lead: An operating system changes with the machine it runs. Early computers ran one job at a time; batch systems grouped jobs to keep the CPU busy; multiprogramming and time-sharing let many jobs or users share one machine; real-time systems meet deadlines; distributed, embedded, mobile and open-source systems serve new settings. Knowing this history explains why an OS has queues, timers, protected memory and scheduling. It also helps you pick the right type: a ventilator needs real-time behaviour, a ticket server needs time-sharing, and a phone needs a mobile OS.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for what an OS does, and the basic idea of interrupts from Chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: Early computers had no operating system in the modern sense. A programmer loaded a program by setting switches or plugging cables, and the machine ran one job at a time. This is serial processing: one job owns the central processing unit (CPU) from start to finish. Setup time was large and the CPU sat idle while a human prepared the next job.

Batch processing added a resident monitor, a small program that stayed in memory. The operator collected similar jobs onto a tape or disk, and the monitor loaded each job in turn. Jobs were written in job control language: a few control cards told the monitor what to run, what data to use and what to do at the end. Batch systems raised CPU use and removed the programmer from the machine room, but a user could not interact with a running job. Debugging meant reading a printed listing later.

Hardware generations shaped these designs. First-generation machines used vacuum tubes. Second-generation machines used transistors, third-generation machines used integrated circuits, and fourth-generation machines used very large-scale integration (VLSI). The fourth generation also brought the personal computer (PC). Each step gave more memory and faster input/output (I/O), which made multiprogramming practical. Some syllabi call this the 'history and evolution' part of the course. The main lesson is not the dates: each OS feature appears when hardware makes it affordable.

Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in main memory at once. When the running job waits for an I/O device, the OS switches the CPU to another ready job. The CPU stays busy and throughput (completed jobs per unit time) rises. The cost is more memory, a job scheduler and careful protection between jobs. See Unit 2, Process Scheduling, for the algorithms.

Time-sharing is multiprogramming built for interaction. The OS gives each user a short turn, called a time slice, then switches. A timer interrupt forces the switch, so one user cannot keep the CPU. Each user sees a slow but responsive machine. Time-sharing needs a timer and dual mode, covered in Chapter 1.4.

Multitasking is time-sharing applied to one user's tasks: a phone plays music while a chat app checks messages. Multiprocessing uses two or more CPUs or cores to run work in parallel. Do not use the words as synonyms. Multiprogramming is about keeping the CPU busy during I/O; multitasking is about one user running several tasks; multiprocessing is about more than one processor.

sections.h3: Real-time, distributed, embedded, mobile and open-source

blocks.text: Real-time systems have a correctness condition beyond the answer: the result must arrive by a deadline. A hard real-time system fails if a deadline is missed; a ventilator or car brake controller is an example. A soft real-time system degrades when late; video streaming or online gaming is an example. Real-time OSes use priority scheduling and bounded interrupt latency, the longest time before the OS answers a device. Scheduling details are in Unit 2.

A distributed OS manages several computers so that they look like one system. Users do not care which machine holds a file or runs a process. It needs distributed synchronization and distributed file systems; see Unit 6. A network OS is weaker: each machine runs its own OS and users know the machine names.

An embedded OS runs inside a device with limited memory, power and display: a washing machine, router or drone controller. It often has real-time parts. A mobile OS is an embedded-style OS with a rich interface. It manages touch input, radio and battery, sandboxes apps and limits background work. Android and iOS are common examples.

Open-source systems publish source code under a licence that allows study, change and redistribution. Linux and Android are open source. Open source is a licensing property, not a scheduling type; an open-source OS can be batch, server, mobile or real-time. Virtualization and cloud computing now put many OS instances on one server; see Chapter 1.9.

figure.caption: The bars show when each type dominated; batch ends where time-sharing begins, and time-sharing overlaps the PC era from 1980 to 1985. The PC and mobile bars meet at 2000.

spec.aria: A timeline showing batch systems, time-sharing, personal computers and mobile operating systems overlapping in different eras.

examples.question: The timeline gives batch 1950–1965, time-sharing 1965–1985, PC 1980–2000 and mobile 2000–2025. (a) Find the overlap in years between time-sharing and PC systems. (b) Find the full span from the start of batch to the end of mobile. (c) Which of the four types first allowed a user to interact directly with a running job?
steps: Write the intervals as (start, end): time-sharing (1965, 1985), PC (1980, 2000).

Use overlap = max(0, min(end₁, end₂) − max(start₁, start₂)); start₁ and end₁ are the time-sharing interval's start and end, and start₂ and end₂ are the PC interval's. Here min(1985, 2000) = 1985 and max(1965, 1980) = 1980, so overlap = 1985 − 1980 = 5 years.
Full span = end of mobile − start of batch = 2025 − 1950 = 75 years.
Batch jobs ran without interaction. Time-sharing gave each user a terminal and a time slice, so the user could type commands and see replies while the job ran. Answer to (c): time-sharing.
examples.answer: The overlap is 5 years, the full span is 75 years, and time-sharing first gave a user direct interaction with a running job.
examples.check:
ts_start, ts_end = 1965, 1985
pc_start, pc_end = 1980, 2000
overlap = max(0, min(ts_end, pc_end) - max(ts_start, pc_start))
span = 2025 - 1950
print(overlap)
print(span)

traps: Batch vs time-sharing: batch runs jobs without interaction; time-sharing gives each user a time slice and a terminal.
Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory; multitasking is time-sharing on one user's work; multiprocessing uses more than one CPU.
Hard real-time is not 'fast'. It is 'meets every deadline'. A fast system can still be soft if it has no deadline guarantee.
A distributed OS gives a single-system view. A network OS lets separate machines share resources while each keeps its own OS.
Open source is not the same as freeware. Open source gives rights to the source code; freeware may be closed and only free of charge.

quiz.a: Batch processing groups jobs with similar needs and runs them one after another under a resident monitor, without direct user interaction.

quiz.q: Why does time-sharing need a timer interrupt?
quiz.a: The timer ends each user's time slice and forces the CPU back to the OS, so one user cannot keep the CPU while others wait.

quiz.q: Using the timeline, how many years pass from the start of the PC era in 1980 to the end of the mobile era in 2025?
A ventilator's OS must produce a control output within 10 ms; a late output can harm the patient. Is this hard or soft real-time, and what follows for scheduling?
quiz.a: Hard real-time, because a missed deadline is a failure. The OS must bound interrupt latency and use priority scheduling; average speed alone is not enough.

quiz.q: State one difference between multiprogramming and multiprocessing.
quiz.a: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory on one CPU and switches during I/O waits; multiprocessing uses two or more CPUs or cores to run work in parallel.

quiz.q: Classify each setting: (i) an IRCTC server handling many users' booking sessions, (ii) one phone playing music while a chat app runs, (iii) a drone flight controller, (iv) bank branch computers that appear as one file system.
An OS is released as open source. Does that guarantee it is real-time? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Open source is a licence for source code. Real-time behaviour depends on bounded interrupt latency, priority scheduling and worst-case timing, which the licence does not provide.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems push these ideas further: cloud hypervisors run many virtual machines; containers share one kernel; unikernels build a tiny single-purpose OS; and real-time Linux adds bounded-latency patches for robots and cars. Mobile OSes use low-memory killers and background limits to protect battery and response time. Search for 'unikernel', 'PREEMPT_RT', 'seL4 microkernel' and 'Android low-memory killer' to go deeper.
